newsitem.title: USA: Lake vows keep Congress clued in on intelligence.
newsitem.headline: Lake vows keep Congress clued in on intelligence.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's choice to head the troubled CIA vowed on Tuesday to provide unvarnished intelligence to decision makers and do even more than mandated by law to keep Congress informed if confirmed by the Senate.

At the start of twice-postponed, politically sensitive confirmation hearings, Anthony Lake said his previous job as Clinton's first-term national security adviser would not keep him from presenting the hard truth.

"Some have asked whether I -- as a close associate of President Clinton and participant in policy discussions -- can and will provide him the intelligence straight," he told the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence.
"This is indeed an appropriate question. The answer, unequivocably, is 'yes'," Lake went on. "I know first-hand how important it is to defend the bright line separating policy and intelligence."

In opening statements foreshadowing a bruising confirmation process, several Republicans cited concern about foreign policy issues over which Lake held sway, including the decision to keep Congress in the dark about Clinton's tacit approval of Iranian arms shipments to Bosnian Moslems in 1994.

"I have no apologies for the (Bosnia arms) policy," Lake said in his opening statement. "But I do appreciate that it would have been better to have informed key members of Congress on a discreet basis."

As director of central intelligence, Lake would head the Central Intelligence Agency and take overall responsibility for its 12 companion espionage outfits that together account for about $30 billion in annual outlays.
"I pledge to you that, if confirmed, I will not only fulfil every legal requirement in keeping Congress informed, but will go beyond." When in doubt, he said, "my rule would be to inform" lawmakers.
He said he would like to meet intelligence committee members monthly "to discuss the problems on your minds as well as mine, and to work those problems through at as early a stage as possible."

Lake would be Clinton's third CIA director and the fifth person to hold the job in less than six years. He said the intelligence community has suffered from "turbulence and scandal," a possible reference to two convicted turncoats, an oft-changing leadership and disclosure of botched covert operations in Iraq and elsewhere.
Lake reiterated his previously stated intention to stay on as the nation's spy chief for four full years -- "the president, the Congress and fate willing."

Sen. Richard Shelby of Alabama, the Republican chairman of the intelligence panel, began the questioning by asking Lake whether he knew about the FBI's concerns over China's alleged plan to influence the 1996 presidential and congressional elections.

Lake said he had not been informed about the China matter by two of his staff who were briefed by the FBI. He said he should have been told, but declined to criticise the staff members because the matter was still under investigation.
Lake conceded Shelby's point that, as head of the National Security Council staff, he should be held accountable for any management failures there that may be turned up.

"Most important, if confirmed, I will promote from day one a climate of total accountability," Lake said in his opening statement. He said as head of the CIA he would demand that his subordinates keep him and the president "properly informed."
"And if any officials fail to do so, there must be a clear response: He or she will need to find another job."
